# Playbook for ref_estate

**On purchasing property:**
When I land on an unowned property, I buy it if I have sufficient cash and it costs less than half my current balance. This preserves liquidity for rent payments while building my portfolio.

When I land on an unowned property in the final lap, I buy only if I have cash to spare after accounting for potential rent I might owe. On the final lap, unowned properties are less valuable since I won't collect rent from them.

**On cash management:**
I track my declared balance plus all recent transfers before deciding on purchases. I do not commit to buying a property if it would leave me with less than 50 in cash, since I need reserves to pay rent to other investors.

**On property strategy:**
Early in the game, I prioritize acquiring properties that generate moderate to high rent returns (15+ per rental). Properties under 100 in cost are attractive because they allow portfolio diversification without excessive cash drain.

Properties over 100 in cost require careful evaluation—I only purchase them if my cash balance is clearly sufficient and I'm not in the final two laps where I won't collect rent from them.

**On rent obligations:**
When I land on another investor's property, I pay immediately and accept this as a cost of the game. I do not factor "what if I had bought this instead" into my decision-making; I focus on optimizing future moves.

**On final position:**
I do not attempt purchases I cannot afford. In the final lap especially, I declare my balance conservatively and accept that some properties will pass to others.

# My ref_estate Playbook

**On the decision to buy an unowned property:**

When I land on an unowned property in the early laps (1-3), I will buy it if it costs less than half my current cash. Properties generate steady rent income over multiple laps, and early acquisition compounds this advantage. The rent-to-price ratio matters less than securing deed ownership when cash is plentiful.

When I land on an unowned property in the mid-to-late laps (4-6), I will decline to buy. By this point, the remaining lap count doesn't justify the capital outlay, and I should preserve cash for my final score calculation.

**On passing START:**

When I pass or land on START, I will immediately add the salary (25) to my running mental total before declaring my balance. I nearly failed to account for this once—treat salary collection as automatic and mandatory to track.

**On paying rent:**

When I land on an owned property, I will calculate: (last declared balance + any received transfers since last turn) - rent owed. I will always pay what is owed. Do not attempt to avoid rent or negotiate; the bank holds deeds and the rule is firm.

**On my final score:**

Remember that my score is my declared cash plus the purchase price of all deeds I hold. I ended with one deed (Wharf, 80) and 111 cash, totaling 191. In future games, I should track not just cash but also the cumulative value of my property portfolio throughout all six laps. A property-heavy strategy early may outperform a cash-preservation strategy late.

**On general strategy:**

I played conservatively and ended with modest returns. I should consider being more aggressive with property acquisition earlier and accepting more rent payments as a cost of being in a competitive market. Sitting on cash feels safe but misses the compounding benefit of multiple properties generating rent across six laps.

2.text:
# ref_estate Playbook

**On buying properties:**

When I land on an unowned property, I buy it if I can afford it and still maintain at least 50 cash buffer for rent payments. Early properties are especially valuable because I'll collect rent throughout the remaining laps. Don't be afraid to spend down to acquire income-generating assets in the first half of the game.

When I land on an unowned property late in the game (final lap or two) and my cash is tight, I decline the purchase. The opportunity cost of immobilizing capital is too high when there are few laps remaining to recoup the investment through rent collection.

**On cash management:**

I maintain a running total of my actual cash position by tracking: last declared balance + received payments - outgoing payments. I do this calculation before each decision, not after. The bank's record shows what happened; I declare what I now have.

When I declare a balance, I account for all recent transfers since my last turn, not just the current turn's transaction.

**On rent payments:**

When I land on an owned property, I pay the rent immediately without hesitation if I have the funds. I prioritize maintaining liquidity to handle future rent obligations.

**On the final calculation:**

My score is my declared cash plus the purchase price of all deeds I hold. This means buying properties early, even at significant cash cost, converts my liquid assets into scoring assets. Properties I buy for 60-100 will score at their full purchase price regardless of how much cash I finish with.
